title: About Time
by: Richard Curtis (writer-director); Domhnall Gleeson, Rachel McAdams, Bill Nighy
summary: A romantic comedy that uses a deliberately simple time-travel rule to turn, halfway through, into a family drama about a dying father and the value of living an ordinary day.

title: Autumn Sonata
by: Ingmar Bergman (writer-director); Sven Nykvist (cinematography); Ingrid Bergman, Liv Ullmann, Lena Nyman
summary: A chamber film in which one Chopin prelude, played first by a daughter and then by her famous mother, holds a whole relationship, and a single night of talk becomes the climax.

title: La Notte
by: Michelangelo Antonioni (director); Gianni Di Venanzo (cinematography); Giorgio Gaslini (music); Marcello Mastroianni, Jeanne Moreau, Monica Vitti
summary: A day and a night in a dying marriage, told almost entirely through images: figures dwarfed by Milan's new architecture, faces behind glass, a long silent walk, and a dawn ending that withholds the climax.

title: The Lord of the Rings
by: Peter Jackson (director); screenplays by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens and Peter Jackson (with Stephen Sinclair on The Two Towers), from J. R. R. Tolkien; music by Howard Shore
summary: A nine-hour quest that braids three strands toward one fixed destination, restructures its source with care, lets leitmotifs carry memory, and ends with a hero who cannot go home.

title: Prometheus
by: Ridley Scott (director); screenplay by Jon Spaihts and Damon Lindelof; Michael Fassbender, Noomi Rapace, Charlize Theron
summary: An honest double lesson: superb design, a model character introduction in David and a set piece built on a want under pressure, undermined by decisions that come from the plot rather than the characters.

title: Spirited Away
by: Hayao Miyazaki (writer-director), Studio Ghibli; music by Joe Hisaishi
summary: A coming-of-age fantasy whose heroine grows through work and kindness rather than combat, set in a bathhouse whose rules are the plot, with Miyazaki's deliberate pauses (ma) doing as much as the action.

title: Uptown Girls
by: Boaz Yakin (director); Brittany Murphy, Dakota Fanning, Heather Locklear
summary: A critically panned but much-loved odd-couple film in which a childlike heiress and an adult-like eight-year-old swap what each lacks, built on Snyder's Buddy Love and a teacup ride that pays off a plant.

title: World War Z
by: Marc Forster (director); screenplay by Matthew Michael Carnahan, Drew Goddard and Damon Lindelof, from the novel by Max Brooks; Brad Pitt, Mireille Enos
summary: A zombie epic rebuilt as a globe-trotting investigation, whose scrapped battle finale was replaced by a near-silent climax in a lab corridor: a lesson in sequences, scale versus intimacy, and adapting an oral history into a single hero's quest.

title: The Worst Person in the World
by: Joachim Trier (director; co-writer with Eskil Vogt); Renate Reinsve, Anders Danielsen Lie, Herbert Nordrum
summary: A coming-of-age film told in a prologue, twelve titled chapters and an epilogue, whose wry narrator, elastic sense of time and a city frozen mid-stride show how the telling can carry a heroine who won't choose.
